Business.title: More funding needed to boost construction jobs for young people - housing boss
Business.text:
A long-term plan and additional funding is needed to create more placements for young people within the construction industry, according to one housing association boss.

Iwan Trefor Jones, chief executive at Adra, said it was important that organisations worked together to make sure "that there are opportunities for young people".

Adra had seen a rise in demand in its academy scheme, with one of their recent openings attracting 108 applicants for only six positions.

The Welsh government said work was already under way "to boost construction skills" and new apprenticeships were set to launch later in the year.

Recent analysis by the Federation of Master Builders showed that the construction sector was facing a shortfall of labour and needed an additional 2,200 workers a year in order to meet demand.

Steven Walker, a construction manager with Williams Homes, said it was "really important" that more young people came into the construction industry.

"We have an ageing workforce across the country" he said. "It's really important that young people are being pushed through to be work ready... to be the next generation of construction workers."

There was always room for more workers, he added.

"We can always create the space for young people to come and work on our construction sites.

"We buddy them up with an experienced worker, we show them the ropes, we give them the training, we look after them, we interview them regularly to see that they're OK and that they're looked after."

Speaking at one of Adra's developments of over 58 social and affordable homes in Bangor, Jones said additional funding was needed to give more young people opportunities to get into the sector.

"There's a need for a long-term plan, but also a plan is nothing without the funding behind it," he said.

"We need some kind of assurance that there is a long-term plan to support the funding of placements in work, to support young people into employment and to support employers."

The Academi Adra scheme was established in 2021 with the aim of providing young people with skills and experience in the workplace, offering courses in construction.

Two-hundred-and-thirty participants have been supported since the launch of the scheme, with the most recent course having 108 applicants for only six positions.

Elin Williams, who oversees the work of the Academi, said funding had been needed to offer more young people the chance to join similar schemes.

She said: "We've been very lucky to be able to have some external grant funding to allow us to run some courses and pay for placement opportunities.

"We're calling for more funding for opportunities and projects like Academi Adra... We want to carry on to develop and expand to meet the rising demand that we're seeing."

In recent months, Welsh figures, external suggested the proportion of young people in Wales who are not in education, employment, or training (Neet) had risen sharply.

They increased to 17% and returned to levels last seen around 2013, according to Welsh government figures.

Cian Halliday, 26, a carpenter from Llanrug, had been made redundant during the Covid-19 pandemic, something he said had been "difficult, and a struggle".

"Academi Adra were offering courses, and almost 16 weeks of work experience and at the end they decided to keep me on as a labourer. I did that for a year," he said.

"Then they offered me an apprenticeship and I chose to be a carpenter."

He said that being made redundant had been very tough.

"It was difficult, and a struggle to find work, so I decided, the minute this opportunity came up, to start a new job."

While looking for work, Cian said there had not been enough opportunities for young people like him.

"I was happy enough to change careers. I jumped at the opportunity and never looked back," he said.

Daniella Williams, 35 also got into the construction industry after a period of not being in work following an illness.

"I used to work within the NHS. I had problems with my health and I had children, so left that job, and I really wanted to get into an office-based job," she said.

Williams followed a course with Academi Adra to get into an administrative role.

"It's changed mine and my children's lives... I've been able to save, I've bought my own car, and it's given me so much more confidence," she said.

"I've been able to achieve so much that I wasn't able to before, and it's inspired my children as well to go on and do bigger and better than myself."

Williams said she was also passionate about helping inspire young girls to follow careers in the construction industry.

"'I work with schools... especially to get girls into construction.

"It's not just bricks and building, there are all kinds of different things. We work a lot with local companies, and it's a great sector to get into, I really enjoy it."

With the rise in demand for homes to be built, CHC said that opportunities needed to be made to end the "housing emergency".

Clarissa Corbisiero, deputy chief executive at CHC, said: "Investing in our homes is the best investment we can make in Wales' economic health.

"In building 20,000 new social homes over the next four years, housing associations can deliver over 14,000 jobs per year during construction.

"By aligning our housing goals with a bold construction skills strategy, we can turn a national emergency into a wave of opportunity for every community.

"Ending the housing emergency is more than bricks and mortar - it's about health, jobs and opportunity."

The Welsh government said: "We are committed to developing a Welsh skills system fit for the future. Work is already under way to boost construction skills with Level 2 apprenticeships in bricklaying, site carpentry, scaffolding and building maintenance set to launch later this year.

"Construction will also be included in new VCSE qualifications from September 2027.

"A skills audit is currently under way to provide a clear, cross government view of current and future workforce needs across Wales.

"A future Skills Summit is being held this October that will bring together employers, educators, training providers and policymakers to help shape reforms to vocational skills training in Wales."

Business.title: ‘The most anti-union president’: how Trump turned his back on US workers
Business.text:
Donald Trump has repeatedly vowed to champion US workers. Shortly before Labor Day last year, he said: “Every policy of the Trump administration is designed to lift up the American worker and “promote great-paying blue-collar jobs”. But in the year since last Labor Day, Trump has taken many actions that have hurt US workers and unions, with some labor experts saying they’ve been stunned at how anti-worker Trump has been.

In the months after Trump returned to office, the Occupational Safety and Health Administration (Osha) cut workplace inspections by 20%, compared with Joe Biden’s last year in office. Even though Trump campaigned as a champion of coal miners, his administration has repeatedly delayed implementation of a rule to limit silica dust, which has afflicted and killed many coal miners with black lung. The United Mine Workers union has urgently called for “immediate enforcement” of the stalled silica dust rule.

With regard to wages, workers haven’t been doing so well under Trump. While the White House boasts that wages have risen, the problem for workers is that prices – pushed up by Trump’s tariffs and the Iran war – have risen faster than wages over the past year, helping fuel the affordability crisis. In a move that will cut pay for many low-wage workers, the Trump administration has proposed eliminating federal minimum wage and overtime protections for 3 million often low-paid homecare workers who take care of seniors and the disabled.

Despite several court rulings to slow or stop this anti-union effort, Trump has pushed aggressively ahead with his unprecedented campaign to strip 1 million federal employees of their ability to bargain collectively – a move that Liz Shuler, president of the AFL-CIO, the nation’s main labor federation, called, “the largest single act of union-busting in our history”. Trump has moved to end collective bargaining for hundreds of thousands of workers at the Transportation Security Agency, the Department of Veterans Affairs, the Department of Agriculture, the Environmental Protection Agency and other agencies.

In another unprecedented move, Trump fired Gwynne Wilcox, the pro-union chair of the National Labor Relations Board – the first time a president has fired an NLRB member. Trump has since named numerous pro-business officials to the labor board.

“Trump’s actions make him by far the most anti-union president in our modern history,” Sara Nelson, president of the Association of Flight Attendants and a leading progressive voice in the labor movement, said in an interview. “His administration has been massively anti-worker, anti-union and anti-working class.”

White House officials take sharp issue with critics who say Trump is anti-worker. Taylor Rogers, a White House spokesperson, said: “President Trump will always put American workers first, which is why he signed the largest middle-class tax cuts in history, secured trillions in investments into our country, and negotiated historic trade deals to reshore our manufacturing industry and protect American jobs. Thanks to President Trump, American workers are prioritized over illegal aliens and foreign-born workers once again.”

Heidi Shierholz, president of the Economic Policy Institute, a progressive thinktank, said she was stunned by some of Trump’s anti-worker actions, especially by his order last year chopping the minimum wage that federal contractors must pay their employees, to $13.30 an hour from $17.75. That move caused some workers to lose over $9,000 a year in pay.

This year, Trump rescinded a Biden-era regulation that made overtime pay available to more salaried workers. As a result, 4.3 million workers will no longer qualify for time-and-a-half overtime. (Two federal courts in Texas had ruled against Biden’s overtime regulation.) In his years as president, Trump has never pushed to raise the $7.25-an-hour federal minimum wage, which has greatly eroded in value since it last increased in 2009.

“The Trump administration is systematically weakening policies and institutions that give workers a voice, that give workers protections and that hold employers accountable,” Shierholz said. “He’s been doing that from day one, and since then it has absolutely continued and accelerated. You see attacks on every kind of worker protection from safety and health to wage and hour protections. Policy after policy after policy goes directly against the interests of workers.”

Trump has helped some groups of workers by getting Congress to enact no tax on tips and a significant cut in taxes on overtime pay. The White House boasts that Trump also helped cuts taxes for working families, but Trump’s critics say those cuts overwhelmingly favor the ultra-wealthy, while giving just modest cuts to workers.

President Biden had proposed a landmark regulation to protect workers against extreme heat, but the Trump administration, pushed hard by corporate America, is seeking to seriously weaken Biden’s effort to require rest breaks for workers and access to water and shade when it is very hot. The Trump administration also wants to undo Biden’s plans to codify extreme heat as a workplace hazard.

This past February, after intense lobbying by corporations, the Trump administration moved to scrap a Biden-era rule and make it far easier for employers to classify workers as independent contractors, be they construction workers or Uber drivers. This move will significantly lower many employers’ labor costs by removing any obligation to pay minimum wage and overtime and to contribute to those workers’ Social Security, Medicare and unemployment insurance benefits.

Although Trump boasts that the US economy is in the best shape ever, monthly job growth under Trump is down significantly compared with Biden. Young workers are having a hard time finding jobs, while Trump has been an outspoken cheerleader for AI and datacenters, which are fueling huge fears about many jobs disappearing. Trump promised to use tariffs and other means to make American manufacturing great again. But ever since Trump returned to office, the US has lost 35,000 manufacturing jobs, partly because of all the chaos and uncertainty Trump’s tariffs created, although in the past few months there have been modest gains in factory jobs.

The Trump administration has shown hostility to unions in a way that shocked many Americans. As part of an investigation into opposition to ICE’s operations in Minnesota, Trump’s Department of Homeland Security got hold of financial records from two leading unions, the Service Employees International Union and the Communications Workers of America, saying that this was part of an inquiry into “domestic terrorism financing”.

Further showing how much Trump officials dislike and distrust organized labor, Trump’s prosecutors even told a grand jury that the AFL-CIO, the nation’s main union federation, representing 15 million American workers and retirees, and several unions were part of a criminal conspiracy to obstruct the efforts of ICE agents in Minnesota.

“It’s terrible that they’re going after labor activists and unions in Minnesota for merely standing up for their neighbors,” Nelson said. “It’s outrageous that this administration called union members who are fighting for their neighbors ‘domestic terrorists’.”

Business.title: ‘There’s no plan’: as instability in global bond markets rises, what are the knock-on effects?
Business.text:
When Donald Trump was asked recently about the threat of rising interest rates on US government debt, he told baffled reporters: “The ultimate intervention is our military. And if we have to use that, we will.”

Perhaps not surprisingly, his bellicose words did not soothe fractious bond markets, and his resumption of the bombing campaign against Iran only made matters worse.

The past fortnight has seen a wave of instability sweeping through government bond markets in major economies – with knock-on effects for millions of borrowers. The interest rate, or yield, on 10-year US government borrowing hit 4.8% on Friday, up from 4.64% 10 days ago. At one point midweek, the 30-year yield touched its highest level since 2008.

Neil Shearing, the chief economist at the consultancy Capital Economics, said one impetus for the current wobble had been markets taking a fresh look at the state of US public finances. “There’s been a recalibration,” he said.

Total US government debt has surged past $40tn (£29.5tn), and annual deficits are forecast to be an eye-watering 6% of GDP for the foreseeable future.

Such figures were long deemed barely to matter given the status of US government bonds, or treasuries, as the ultimate safe-haven investment. But as the events that led up to the 2008 financial crisis revealed, things don’t matter in the markets until they do.

“I think we are starting to see a more realistic reassessment of the fiscal pressure in the US,” Shearing said. “What marks the US out is that there’s not really an acknowledgment of the fact that there might be a problem. There’s no plan.”

Russell Jones, a veteran bond market analyst at Llewellyn Consulting, said: “The thing about economics is that often markets delay the judgment and, you know, you can’t really time when they suddenly decide that that’s enough.”

The US treasury secretary Scott Bessent’s recent fumbled attempts to intervene in financial markets – to help Tokyo prop up the yen and then to calm bond yields – have only added to the sense that policymakers are panicking.

Layered on top of these concerns is a more immediate worry about inflation taking off again as a result of renewed hostilities in the Middle East. Oil prices have risen back above $90 a barrel since the US and Iran resumed tit-for-tat attacks.

That has increased expectations that central banks will have to raise interest rates – another factor that puts upward pressure on yields.

Every pronouncement by policymakers is being closely scrutinised for clues, including a key speech by the new Federal Reserve chair, Kevin Warsh, last Friday that was read by markets as signalling a willingness to act.

The European Central Bank is expected to lead the charge with a rate rise next week, but markets are telegraphing higher borrowing costs across major economies.

That includes the UK, where investors are now pencilling in three quarter-point rate rises over the next 12 months, and Japan, where the decades-long period of deflation and rock-bottom rates is finally coming to an end.

A dramatic expansion of borrowing by AI “hyperscalers” in the US, to help fund the massive planned expansion of datacentres, has offered investors an alternative home for their cash – and raised questions about the market’s ability to absorb so much debt simultaneously.

Recent calculations by the investment group Vanguard put the value of debt issued by five major tech companies at $135bn (£100bn) this year, up from an average of $35bn between 2020 and 2024.

There is potentially an even more fundamental explanation for an upward shift in borrowing costs, too – based on the growing prevalence of inflationary shocks not just as a result of geopolitical chaos but because of the climate emergency.

Some economists, including the Bank of England policymaker Swati Dhingra, have argued these increasingly regular shocks, as a result of extreme weather events and resulting economic upheaval, could lead to structurally higher interest rates.

Whatever the causes of rising bond yields, the impact is already rippling out worldwide. Public borrowing has increased dramatically in recent years as policymakers have stepped in to cushion consumers against Covid shutdowns, wrestled with sharply higher energy prices since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, and stepped up defence spending. That means small changes in global interest rates can have an outsized impact on government budgets.

In the UK, where £1 in every £12 of public spending already goes on debt interest, Andy Burnham, the prime minister, was pressed this week by the opposition leader, Kemi Badenoch, about the rising cost of government borrowing.

Higher yields on gilts, as UK government bonds are known, will feed through into predictions of higher interest rate costs for the Treasury ahead of the new chancellor John Healey’s autumn budget.

David Aikman, the director of the National Institute of Economic and Social Research, urged the government to take the opportunity to implement spending cuts and/or tax increases to help insulate the UK from higher borrowing costs.

“There will be a lot of talk about the fiscal rules. I think that’s slightly missing the point,” he said. “The big point here is we’ve just got a lot of debt, whether you’re missing the rules or not. And it means we’re really vulnerable.”

On the other side of the world, Australian policymakers have been wrestling with similar challenges. Bond yields have breached 15-year highs just days after the country passed A$1tn in government debt.

The timing of the two milestones comes at a difficult time for a Labor government that is under pressure to rein in historically high levels of spending.

Falling house prices in a property-obsessed nation are adding to a mood of discontent. Bets have firmed that the Reserve Bank of Australia could deliver another interest rate hike later this month to tame stubbornly high inflation.

Jim Chalmers, the treasurer, has been at pains to highlight Australia’s relatively strong budget position internationally. Australia’s debt is equivalent to about half the size of the economy, which pales against other advanced nations. Similarly, the commonwealth is running deficits, but of less than 1% of GDP.

Chris Richardson, an independent budget expert, said Australia’s government indebtedness wasn’t “bad by world standards”. “But it’s still a lot of debt. And the higher cost of money means the difficult choices that were there already are that much harder.”

For developing countries, these issues are all the more urgent. The International Monetary Fund warned earlier this year that these economies had become more exposed to the risk of higher interest rates, because of the growing importance of lending from short-term investors such as hedge funds, which tend to be more flighty during periods of market volatility.

Matthew Martin, of the advocacy group Development Finance International, said: “A lot of these countries are very near the edge, and if they have to go back to the markets and refinance another bond at 1% or 2% higher than it was before, that will mean even less money to spend on climate action, health and education.”

If higher yields are sustained, the effects will be felt far beyond the world’s treasuries, muddying the maths for corporate investments and putting upward pressure on mortgage rates, which in the UK have already started to rise.

Aikman argued corporate balance sheets worldwide looked less shaky than before the global financial crisis. “We’re not in the place we were in the run-up to 2008,” he said. But he pointed to “pockets” of concern, including the huge scale of debt-fuelled private equity projects that could prove vulnerable in a world of higher rates.

By the end of the week, the sell-off sweeping global bond markets appeared to have eased, for now. But it left yields at levels significantly higher than three months ago – and delivered a painful reminder to policymakers, including Burnham, that in globalised financial markets their plans can be buffeted by forces far beyond their control.

Business.title: Maria Bartiromo’s lawyer denies she was fired from Fox News anchor role
Business.text:
Maria Bartiromo’s lawyer sharply denied that she was fired from her job at Fox News on Friday, after reports that she was dismissed after divulging the network’s editorial guidance to the White House.

Fox announced Bartiromo’s departure on Thursday but provided no explanation, saying only in a statement that it was effective immediately.

“Effective today, Maria Bartiromo is no longer with FOX News Media,” the network said in a press release, adding in a statement: “We thank Maria for her work over the last 12 and a half years and wish her all the best on her next chapter.”

She had been with Fox for more than 12 years and hosted a popular three-hour weekday morning show for the Fox Business network, as well as a Sunday morning show.

Status News reported on Thursday that Fox instructed senior employees to avoid covering Donald Trump’s July primetime address, where he shared unproven and false claims about the 2020 election. Bartiromo, an avid Trump supporter, shared that message with the White House, according to Status News, a violation of company policy. Bartiromo was taken off the air shortly after.

In a statement, Bryan Freedman, Bartiromo’s attorney, called her, “one of the hardest-working journalists throughout her award-winning career” and denied the claims reported by Status News. Freedman has previously defended several journalists fired from their networks, including Don Lemon at CNN, Megyn Kelly at NBC News and Tucker Carlson at Fox.

“The irresponsible reports that have been published stating that Maria Bartiromo was fired or is no longer an employee of Fox are absolutely and unequivocally false,” Freedman said in a statement. “Make no mistake, we have the receipts and witnesses and they will come out whether through the courthouse or otherwise. Those reporting her firing or the incredulous facts supporting that fiction have exhibited a complete and utter reckless disregard for the truth.”

A Fox spokesperson pointed to the company’s original statement and said: “The release speaks for itself.”

Several former Fox News employees are now working at the Trump administration, including Trump’s defense secretary, Pete Hegseth. With the recent announcement that Trump’s press secretary, Karoline Leavitt, would be stepping down at the end of August, some have speculated that Bartiromo might be tapped to step into the role.

Business.title: US added 162,000 jobs in August, with unemployment rate holding steady
Business.text:
The US economy added 162,000 jobs in August, an uptick after a sluggish summer for the labor market.

The unemployment rate held steady at 4.1%, still down from its most recent peak of 4.5% last November, according to new data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS). Despite the relative stability of the unemployment rate, the number of new jobs added to the economy has been fluctuating, going from 214,000 in March down to a 21,000 gain in July and then back up in August.

Figures for job growth in June and July were both revised up. After revisions, job growth in June was 31,000 jobs, up from an initial 20,000, and July was revised up by 44,000 jobs, from an initially reported loss of 23,000 to a gain of 21,000.

Economists had predicted gains would be at least 50,000 new jobs. Earlier in the week, the payroll firm ADP reported private companies added 38,000 jobs in August, lower than initial expectations and the lowest month for new jobs since January. Meanwhile, outplacement firm Challenger, Gray & Christmas reported that layoffs have been going down and are 41% lower than cuts that were announced by this time last year.

Economists have pointed out that the labor market appears to be stalled in a “slow hire, slow fire” state, with neither growth nor contractions in jobs.

A separate BLS report from earlier this week showed job openings and layoffs had changed little in July. The number of people quitting their jobs also remained flat, suggesting workers are feeling less confident about their ability to find another job.

For many Americans feeling frustrated about the economy, a lackluster job market feels especially painful when paired with rising prices. US inflation has increased significantly since the start of the war with Iran, with the annual inflation rate going from 2.4% in February to 3.4% in July. In May, price increases reached 4.2%, the highest rate since 2023.

In recent weeks, persistent inflation has started to have a domino effect in the US economy after a sell-off in the US bond market. Yields for US Treasury bonds have been going up since the start of the Iran war, suggesting that investors are concerned about the long-term health of the economy. Higher yields could push up the price of loans, including mortgages, car loans and the interest rate on student debt, making things even more costly for Americans.

Economists are expecting at least one interest rate hike from the US Federal Reserve before the end of the year. Higher interest rates could help lower inflation, but at the risk of destabilizing the labor market.

Last week, Kevin Warsh, the Fed chair, gave his debut speech at the Fed’s symposium in Jackson Hole, Wyoming, where he said the Fed was still committed to getting inflation down to its 2% target rate, but held off on making any firm suggestions on the central bank’s next move.

“We must be confident that underlying inflation is moving to our objective, clearly and at sufficient speed,” he said. “Otherwise, we have work to do.”

Donald Trump on Friday celebrated the new job figures and threatened to “stop trading with countries with which we have a deficit” if the Fed doesn’t lower interest rates.

“A STRONG COUNTRY MEANS A LOWER INTEREST RATE –IT’S A BETTER CREDIT… Very simple!” Trump wrote on Truth Social. “We should have the LOWEST RATE of any country in the World, like ‘the old days’.”

Business.title: Nvidia to buy developer platform Hugging Face in $12.9bn deal
Business.text:
Nvidia will buy the popular developer platform Hugging Face for nearly $13bn, betting that support for ⁠open AI models could offset a potential slowdown in demand for the semiconductor giant’s chips.

Shares ⁠in Nvidia were ⁠slightly lower ​after the $12.93bn (£9.57bn) deal – which ranks among its biggest ever – was announced for the database of AI models on Thursday.

Hugging Face, based in New York and backed by the likes of Intel, Advanced Micro Devices and Amazon, was founded in 2016 by the French entrepreneurs Clément Delangue, Julien Chaumond and Thomas Wolf.

Nvidia is already a major open AI player in the US with ⁠its widely used Nemotron model and vocal support for the technology.

Acquiring Hugging Face will give it direct access to a platform developers use to ⁠collaborate and test and share tools, potentially providing insight and data that could help it narrow the ​technology gap with top American and ‌Chinese labs.

“Nvidia gains visibility into customer’s preferences and the AI models they use,” said Naveen Chhabra, principal analyst at Forrester. “They can see which models are trending, what datasets customers are downloading, and the architectures that are gaining traction weeks before they hit mainstream tech news.”

Demand for open-weight models ‌has surged from businesses balking at the steep bill of deploying generative AI. Chinese companies ‌such as DeepSeek, Moonshot and Z.ai have emerged as crucial players with models that can match the best from the US in tasks including generating computer code at a lower cost.

There are fears that some US firms could become reliant on Beijing’s models even as both countries race to dominate a technology they see as crucial to their future. The Trump administration has scrambled to respond to the wave of open models from China, weighing whether to restrict their use while also worrying about stifling American businesses that have taken to using them.

Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s chief executive, was a signatory of an open letter earlier this year from major tech firms that advocated for open models and warned against government regulation that would stifle their use. Huang pledged that Nvidia would keep Hugging Face open after acquiring it.

“Hugging ‌Face will remain an open platform for the entire AI ecosystem,” said Huang, adding that his company’s chips would not be required to ​build on or deploy through Hugging Face.

Under the deal, Nvidia will pay about $11.9bn to Hugging Face investors, while offering an equity-based retention program of up to $1bn for employees who join Nvidia.

For Nvidia, building up its open source business may help it cushion a demand slowdown from customers such as ⁠Meta, OpenAI and Microsoft, which are developing their own AI chips to cut reliance ​on its costly and ​supply-constrained processors. Several Chinese chip-making firms have also made recent advancements that could further disrupt the balance of power within big tech, though they face strict international export controls.

It has been a volatile year in the market for chipmakers, with a chip stock selloff in July wiping $1tn from the market caps of leading firms. Nvidia shares bounced back in August, though, with a strong revenue forecast leading to the second-biggest one-day gain in market history – adding $442bn to the company’s market value.

Business.title: Dutch central bank moves 86 tonnes of gold to UK from US and Canada, citing ‘geopolitical unrest’
Business.text:
The Dutch central bank says it has moved 86 tonnes of its gold reserves out of the US and Canada to London, citing “increasing geopolitical unrest”.

De Nederlandsche Bank (DNB) said gold reserves held in London could be traded more easily than those held in New York and Ottawa.

“This makes it the quickest for DNB to deploy in a crisis situation,” the bank said in a statement on Wednesday.

“With this step, we have improved the deployability of the gold reserves. We assume that we will never need to deploy the gold, but it is nevertheless necessary to strengthen our resilience and preparedness,” said DNB’s president, Olaf Sleijpen.

The total Dutch gold stock amounted to 612.4 tonnes and was valued at €72.2bn ($83.7bn) at the end of 2025, said the DNB.

Before the deployment, the Dutch bank held 31.3% of its gold in New York and 19.7% in Ottawa.

After the move, each country accounted for 18.5% of the Dutch gold reserve.

The share of gold held in London increased from 18.1% to 32.1%. The bank still holds 30.8% of its gold in the Netherlands.

The transfer was carried out partially by buying and selling and partly by physically transferring gold, the bank said.

The bank moved more than 27 tonnes of physical gold from the US and Canada to Zeist.

The same quantity of gold was moved from Zeist to London, preventing the melting down of gold bars.

“By combining buying and selling and physical transport, the risks associated with physically moving a large quantity of gold have been spread,” the DNB said.

The operation took place between March and August of this year, it said.

Laurent Schwartz, president of the Paris-based National Gold Counter, which facilitates gold trading in France, said central banks had been moving their reserves around for about a decade.

“The current political context in the United States might also push certain central banks into favouring other storage locations,” he said.

The London market was the deepest and most liquid, Schwartz said, making it easier to deploy in times of crisis.

“Central banks can more easily lend their gold there to other banking institutions.”

John Plassard, an analyst at Cite Gestion Private Bank, said the Dutch move was intended “for there to be more immediate availability in the event of a crisis”.

For the moment, it was a “fairly one-off move”, but he warned that if other central banks followed suit, it could damage confidence in the US.

At the beginning of the year, there were concerns raised in Germany about the security of its central bank’s reserves in New York.

However, the powerful Bundesbank has decided for the moment not to shift its reserves away from New York.

“The New York Fed is and remains an important storage site for our gold,” the bank told public TV station ARD in January.

Sports.title: Virgin's Richard Branson: Flight price rises due to 'foolish leaders' starting wars
Sports.text:
Virgin Group founder Sir Richard Branson has blamed flight price rises on "foolish leaders" starting wars, in a thinly veiled reference to the US-Israel conflict with Iran.

Middle East tensions have choked the production and transportation of millions of barrels of oil, causing a surge in the price of car and jet fuels, which are made from oil.

In May, Virgin Atlantic added a fuel surcharge to ticket prices in response.

US President Donald Trump has repeatedly defended the conflict as necessary for peace and security long-term.

However, Sir Richard said there was "no need" for the war.

"The Iran conflict was completely unnecessary. There was a nuclear agreement between Iran and the rest of the world that had been negotiated by President Obama and a lot of European people.

"It was working, so there was no need to rip it up... And this war has just resulted in much higher oil prices all over the world. And inflation has been one of the consequences."

The BBC has contacted the White House for comment.

The European benchmark jet fuel price had been hovering around $800 (£590) a tonne but spiked following the outbreak of the Iran war, reaching a peak of over $1,800 in April. It has since dropped to around $1,450.

Virgin Atlantic's chief executive, Corneel Koster, told the BBC that for "this level of fuel price" fuel surcharges were "absolutely required", adding that it's "hard to be optimistic at this moment about the situation in the Middle East".

The surcharge Virgin introduced added £50 to an economy class fare, £180 to premium and £360 to business class.

Sports.title: Can Harry Kane buck Ballon d’Or World Cup history?
Sports.text:
With the Ballon d'Or shortlist to be announced on Tuesday, Harry Kane heads the field as the bookmakers' favourite after a prolific season for club and country. History, however, suggests football's biggest individual prize is rarely decided on goals alone.

Since the Ballon d'Or was first awarded in 1956, performances in the game's biggest competitions have consistently shaped the outcome.

World Cup years, in particular, have followed a remarkably clear pattern and recent editions have shown just how difficult it is to win the award without lifting a major global or continental tournament.

Once the nominees are announced, an international jury of specialised journalists will cast their votes, with one representative per country from the men's top 100 having their say.

So, can Kane, who has never finished higher than 10th in the battle to be the world's best player, become one of the rare exceptions?

Created by France Football journalist Gabriel Hanot, the Ballon d'Or was first presented in 1956, with England's Sir Stanley Matthews the inaugural winner. Originally voted for by journalists, the award was restricted to European players until eligibility was expanded to all nationalities in 1995.

Raymond Kopa became the first Ballon d'Or winner in a World Cup year after helping France reach the 1958 semi-finals. To mark the award's 60th anniversary in 2016, France Football revisited every pre-1995 edition, external. Its retrospective review concluded Pele would have claimed the award after inspiring Brazil to their first World Cup triumph at the age of 17.

Four years later, Josef Masopust officially won the Ballon d'Or after captaining Czechoslovakia to the World Cup final. Again, France Football judged Brazil's Garrincha to have been the standout performer after leading his country to successive World Cup titles.

It reached the same verdict for Pele in 1970 after he inspired Brazil to a third World Cup crown. By then, a clear pattern had emerged. Bobby Charlton (1966), Paolo Rossi (1982), Lothar Matthaus (1990), Zinedine Zidane (1998), Ronaldo (2002) and Fabio Cannavaro (2006) all won the Ballon d'Or after lifting the World Cup.

Even among the official exceptions, players still tended to enjoy deep runs at the tournament. Johan Cruyff collected the Ballon d'Or after leading the Netherlands to the 1974 World Cup final, while Luka Modric repeated the feat with Croatia in 2018.

World Cup success has never been an absolute requirement. Kevin Keegan won the 1978 Ballon d'Or despite England failing to qualify for the World Cup, although France Football later concluded Argentina striker Mario Kempes would have been the deserving winner after finishing as the tournament's top scorer and helping the hosts lift the trophy. The publication reached the same verdict for World Cup winners Diego Maradona in 1986 and Romario in 1994.

France Football's review ultimately reinforced the World Cup's influence on the Ballon d'Or. In essence, had the prize always been open to players from all countries, each South American World Cup-winning side between 1958 and 1994 would have supplied the winner.

The World Cup is not the only competition to shape Ballon d'Or voting.

Recent history suggests success in one of football's biggest tournaments has become almost a prerequisite. Only four of the previous 19 Ballon d'Or winners failed to lift either the Champions League, World Cup, European Championship or Copa America during the year of their triumph.

Those exceptions underline just how extraordinary Lionel Messi and Cristiano Ronaldo had to be. Messi won despite Argentina's quarter-final exit at the 2010 World Cup, and again in 2012 and 2019 without lifting a major international or continental trophy.

Ronaldo also prevailed in 2013 after Portugal failed to progress beyond the World Cup play-offs, thanks largely to another remarkable individual season with Real Madrid.

Conversely, Wesley Sneijder's treble with Inter Milan and run to the 2010 World Cup final, Franck Ribery's role in Bayern Munich's 2013 treble and Mohamed Salah's record-breaking 2017-18 season all proved insufficient when voters favoured different narratives.

Voters might face a familiar dilemma.

Rodri appears Kane's strongest rival. The former Ballon d'Or winner was arguably Spain's standout performer throughout the tournament, collecting the Golden Ball after helping his country secure a second World Cup title.

Lamine Yamal also added a World Cup winner's medal to a season in which he helped Barcelona reclaim La Liga, although it was teenage team-mate Pau Cubarsi who claimed the Fifa Young Player Award after a series of outstanding performances.

Mbappe and Messi are also expected to feature prominently. Mbappe finished as the World Cup's top scorer with 10 goals, while also claiming the Champions League Golden Boot and La Liga's top scorer trophy, despite France falling short of the final and Real Madrid ending the season without a major honour. Messi, meanwhile, captained Argentina to a second successive World Cup final and at the age of 39 scored eight goals during the tournament.

Should Kane prevail, he would become only the fifth Englishman to win the Ballon d'Or after Matthews, Charlton, Keegan and Michael Owen. He would also become the first player representing a Bundesliga club to lift the trophy since Matthias Sammer in 1996.

History suggests the odds remain stacked against him but few players have entered a Ballon d'Or election with stronger individual credentials.

Voters must now decide if one of the most prolific goalscoring seasons of the modern era outweighs football's biggest prizes, and if Kane can join one of the most exclusive groups in Ballon d'Or history.

Sports.title: Pakistan investigate 'discipline and conduct' on turbulent tour
Sports.text:
Pakistan have begun an inquiry into "discipline and conduct" in the latest twist on a turbulent tour of England.

Already 2-0 down in the three-match Test series, Pakistan last week sent seven players home, called up seven more and replaced head coach Sarfaraz Ahmed with New Zealander Mike Hesson.

During the second Test at Lord's, the tourists also threatened to cancel the remainder of the match and the tour over an interview broadcast by Sky with the sons of imprisoned former Pakistan prime minister and captain Imran Khan.

In a statement released on Monday morning, the Pakistan Cricket Board (PCB) said: "The Pakistan Cricket Board has initiated an internal disciplinary inquiry following media reports concerning discipline and conduct, which are currently being reviewed internally.

"The PCB handles such matters in accordance with its standard procedures. The process is being conducted under PCB regulations, ensuring that all concerned individuals are given due consideration."

The statement refers to "speculative reports" from "hostile external sources".

Last week, Hesson responded to reports Salman Ali Agha - one of the seven dropped players - refused to attend a meeting with King Charles at Clarence House.

Hesson also refuted suggestions that Mohammad Imran and Mohammad Imran Jr were both called up as replacements because the PCB was confused by their names.

The statement continued: "At this stage, any speculative reports or unverified claims circulating on certain platforms, particularly those originating from hostile external sources, should not be regarded as credible.

"The PCB will not comment further at this time. The Board advises stakeholders and the public to rely on official PCB communications."

Sports.title: Liverpool transfers: Busy in-tray for next sporting director
Sports.text:
With Richard Hughes' move to Al-Hilal now confirmed, Liverpool are seeking a new sporting director for the fifth time since 2022.

Hughes joined Liverpool in the summer of 2024 and oversaw the appointments of Arne Slot then Andoni Iraola. He informed the club earlier this year that he wanted to pursue a new challenge in Saudi Arabia.

Mike Gordon, the president of Fenway Sports Group (FSG), is overseeing the process of finding Hughes' replacement, with Liverpool keen to make a swift appointment.

Liverpool will look at internal candidates, but have not ruled out the possibility of appointing someone from outside the club. There is a desire to have someone that is committed long term.

But who are candidates? And what challenges do they face?

David Woodfine, who was Hughes' assistant and was previously Liverpool's director of loans is one potential candidate. Woodfine was pictured giving Iraola a tour of the facilities at the AXA Training Centre when he arrived in June.

Another is Julian Ward, who was Liverpool's sporting director between 2022 and 2023 and oversaw the signings of Luis Diaz, Cody Gakpo, Alexis Mac Allister and Darwin Nunez. He is now FSG's technical director.

Pedro Marques is FSG's director of football development and was previously the technical director at Benfica, where he helped sign Enzo Fernandez for £10m and before that, a first-team performance analyst at Manchester City.

Outside Anfield, Luis Campos at Paris St-Germain would be the strongest appointment but he is unlikely to view his immediate future away from the European champions.

Whoever replaces Hughes - who has also taken two members of Liverpool's recruitment staff in Mark Burchill and Craig McKee to the Middle East - they will have plenty to address.

Alisson's deal expires at the end of the season and although Juventus were interested in the Brazil goalkeeper this summer, Liverpool had no intention of letting him leave.

Iraola appointed Alisson one of his vice-captains and the 33-year-old has started in all three of their league games so far. He remains comfortably their best goalkeeper even if he is not at his peak.

Liverpool are not short of options, although Giorgi Mamardashvili has not fully convinced thus far while 18-year-old Lucca Brughmans will arrive next summer from Genk in a deal worth up to £30m but is unlikely to be viewed as an immediate first choice.

Alisson has been one of Liverpool's best players during a period in which they won two Premier League titles and a Champions League and the new sporting director will have to decide whether to try and keep him at Anfield next season.

The same can be said of skipper Virgil van Dijk, who is out of contract next summer. Having lost senior figures Mohamed Salah and Andy Robertson at the end of last season, Liverpool need experience, so losing both Alisson and Van Dijk in the same close season would carry risk.

After an extended break following the World Cup, the 35-year-old has played every minute of Liverpool's league campaign so far and although he may not be quite the force he once was, he is still comfortably one of Europe's best centre-backs.

Jeremy Jacquet, Giovanni Leoni, Ifeanyi Ndukwe and Mor Talla Ndiaye have huge potential and the new sporting director may view Van Dijk as the perfect player for them to learn from.

Iraola believes Liverpool have "good numbers" in midfield despite not strengthening that position over the summer following Curtis Jones' move to Inter Milan.

Faith has been placed in Trey Nyoni to feature more this season and the 19-year-old was one of the standouts of Liverpool's pre-season tour of the USA.

As the fixture list heats up, a lot will be asked of Dominik Szoboszlai, Ryan Gravenberch and Mac Allister, so an injury to any of them could prove a major issue.

As reported last week by BBC Sport, Liverpool have looked at Monaco's Lamine Camara but were not open to buying a midfielder this summer.

That position could become a priority in January or next summer, particularly if it looks likely that there will be no contract extension for Mac Allister, whose deal expires in 2028.

As things stand, there are no talks over a new deal for the Argentina midfielder. That will be another situation for Hughes' successor to pick up.

The area where there is less concern is up front, with Hughes signing Alexander Isak, Florian Wirtz, Hugo Ekitike, Victor Munoz and Bradley Barcola on his watch.

With 18-year-old Rio Ngumoha expected to sign a long-term deal, Liverpool appear well-stocked in that department.

Liverpool eventually decided not to allow Cody Gakpo to leave for Manchester City this summer. The Netherlands forward has one goal and three assists already this season, but if they were able to sign a new winger and received another lucrative bid for Gakpo, that could be a scenario the club revisit.

When the question of stability was put to Billy Hogan, Liverpool's CEO, this summer, he told BBC Sport: "I would send a message that we are in a very healthy place as a football club - the leadership from the ownership is in a very steady place and we're looking forward to the next season and the season ahead."

However this has been a summer where Liverpool have changed managers, welcomed new investors, lost a number of senior players and seen their sporting director leave a year earlier than expected. Michael Edwards, who appointed Hughes, also resigned as FSG's CEO of Football.

Hughes, who is understood to have been influenced by Edwards' departure, was integral in the decision to sack Slot and appoint Iraola and ultimately the new sporting director will have a big say in the Spaniard's future.

When he joined Liverpool, Iraola said he only signed a two-year-deal because he didn't just want to be somewhere because he had a contract.

His relationship with Hughes from their time at Bournemouth played a part in him getting the Liverpool job. Now it will be down to someone else to work in tandem with Iraola as Liverpool look to challenge again.

Global head of football Edu has left Nottingham Forest after just over a year at the City Ground.

The former Arsenal midfielder has not attended a games since February and his exit, with his contract believed to have been terminated, has been expected.

Edu's departure comes after former Olympiacos vice-president Theodore Giannikos was appointed chief executive last week.

He replaced Lina Souloukou, who stepped down from the role at the City Ground at the end of last season.

Sports.title: Neco Williams handball: New video - which VAR did not have - shows ball hitting arms
Sports.text:
New video footage has been released that shows the ball coming off Neco Williams' arm in the lead-up to his disallowed goal in the 0-0 draw against Tottenham Hotspur.

The Nottingham Forest defender bundled the ball home in the 67th minute but video assistant referee Peter Bankes stepped in to rule out the goal for accidental handball.

Williams and Forest manager Oliver Glasner were adamant after the match that there was no proof the ball touched an arm.

While the footage vindicates the VAR's decision, it may not end the arguments about the decision to rule out the goal.

It has been a tough couple of days for Bankes, because while the VAR was 100% confident he had made the correct decision, it has attracted intense media scrutiny.

He will now feel vindicated - but there is one important distinction to make.

The new camera angle was not one of those available to Bankes during the game - so it is unlikely to end the anger from Forest fans over the validity of the intervention, even if we know the VAR was ultimately correct.

On the new footage, Williams touches the ball with his left arm then his right forearm before it goes into the net.

The VAR hub only has access to the broadcast cameras, and this camera was one of several which does not transmit as part of match coverage.

Bankes believed the proof on the angles he had available came from the ripple of Williams' shirt as the ball touched his right forearm.

Former midfielder Danny Murphy said on Match of the Day he could understand the argument for the handball but was not convinced the goal should have been ruled out.

"It's a really tricky one," Murphy said. "Maybe it could be a tiny bit on his sleeve or right forearm. But is it clear and obvious? No. That's the answer."

BBC Sport understands that Pro Ref - the new name for the refereeing body that was previously called Professional Game Match Officials (PGMO) - is completely happy with the decision to rule out the goal.

There is irritation within Pro Ref about how the story has developed, partly because Williams was so unequivocal that the ball had not touched his arm - when there is now evidence to the contrary.

"I've seen the images and the replays and at not one moment did I think I handballed it," Williams told Sky Sports.

"I have seen all the images and at not one moment can you tell that has clearly hit my arms, because it never. I knew straight away I've headed it down in between my arms. It didn't hit my arm."

The feeling is that if Williams had not been so certain with his comments that the criticism would not have been as strong.

The new evidence also shows the ball did not touch his head, although because it all happened in a split second it is conceivable he was not aware of that.

Nottingham Forest have been approached for comment.

Much of the commentary on the incident has centred around the VAR not having evidence of a clear and obvious error as a reason to disallow the goal.

Glasner mentioned it and Williams posted on X to that effect too.

But clear and obvious errors only cover subjective incidents - those that require the referee to go to the pitchside monitor to review an incident.

Factual interventions, such as handball before a goal, are evidence-based judgements made by the VAR.

If the VAR feels they have the proof of an offence, they will disallow the goal.

For all Forest's disquiet, there are plenty of people who believe you can see the handball, and Bankes was clearly one of those.

It shows one of the issues with VAR that can never be solved - even the factual interventions like this are, in truth, subjective. It is one person's judgement that others can disagree with.

A case in point is Benjamin Sesko's goal for Manchester United against Liverpool last season.

The ball looked as if it might have brushed the fingertips of the Slovenia striker before going into the goal, but the VAR Stuart Attwell felt he could not be certain and allowed the goal to stand.

Referees' chief Howard Webb later said the ball "probably does hit the hand" but "the VARs need to see that conclusively".

Attwell did not feel he had proof, but Bankes did.

During pre-season media briefings, Webb said attacking handball was one law he would change - which would mean goals like Williams' would not be ruled out based upon the original evidence.

"The problem is the law forces VARs on every goal to look at what body part the ball went in off," Webb said.

"If you were only to penalise when the attacker deliberately handles the ball or makes himself unjustifiably big - and not have that forensic examination - you could 'check complete' it more quickly.

"It is a law I would definitely look to change. So Pro Ref and the Premier League are going to try and lobby for that to be changed."

VAR is being operated with a lighter touch this season. So far there have been just two subjective interventions at 0.06 per game, compared to 0.15 last season.

However the generally negative narrative around VAR and the tribal nature of football mean its involvement in key incidents attracts widespread attention.

Sports.title: Joshua vs Fury: Tyson Fury says he is looking for new opponent and calls out Oleksandr Usyk
Sports.text:
Tyson Fury claims he is looking for a new opponent for November and has called out Oleksandr Usyk despite being contracted to fight Anthony Joshua next.

The all-British heavyweight showdown is being targeted for November, with both Joshua and Fury signing individual contracts for the contest.

But the issue of where the fight takes place has caused a delay in an official announcement with organisers pushing to stage it in the US rather than Joshua's preferred location of Wembley Stadium.

In an expletive-laden video posted on Instagram, Fury claimed Joshua was backing out of the fight.

"This will only lead me to a fight with Oleksandr Usyk," he said.

"Oleksandr you're his [Joshua's] trainer and his sensei and you know he is weak minded... and that he would never fight the Gypsy King which you have had the guts to do twice.

"You got the decisions last time, fair play to you.

"Good luck to you, let's do it again. Let's run it back in November. The ball is now in your court... do you want to fight me this year, 2026, or are you calling it quits?

"Let me know because I am now looking for a new opponent."

Fury has twice lost to Usyk, with the two-time undisputed heavyweight champion now working with Joshua as part of his training and coaching team.

Sela, Queensberry and Matchroom declined to comment on whether talks had broken down when contacted by BBC Sport.

Sports.title: Ratko Mladic: Red Star fans display tifo of war criminal
Sports.text:
Red Star Belgrade fans unveiled a tifo of war criminal Ratko Mladic before their derby win over Partizan Belgrade on Sunday night.

Mladic, who died in a United Nations prison in August, was given a life sentence for genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity in 2017.

He and his troops were responsible for the systematic killing of the non-Serb population of Bosnia-Herzegovina during the wars in the former Yugoslavia between 1992 and 1995.

He oversaw the massacre of 8,000 men and boys at Srebrenica and a siege of the capital Sarajevo in which more than 10,000 people died.

Red Star have already been fined 90,000 euros (£77,000) this season by Uefa, external after their fans unveiled a banner commemorating Mladic in a Europa League play-off against Czech side FC Viktoria Plzen last month.

Red Star's social media accounts published a video of the tifo and the two teams observing a minute's silence for Mladic, alongside a saluting emoji.

The official X account of Bosnia-Herzegovina's national team replied with an obscenity.

After initially enjoying the protection of Serb president Slobodan Milosevic, who would later die while on trial for genocide himself, Mladic spent more than a decade on the run, eventually being found hiding out in a remote farmhouse.

Sports.title: NFL 2026: What to look out for, including Travis Kelce, Aaron Rodgers and Myles Garrett
Sports.text:
Last season was the NFL's "most unusual" in decades, according to veteran analyst Cris Collinsworth.

The Kansas City Chiefs' dynasty began to crumble while joint Super Bowl favourites Baltimore, Buffalo and Philadelphia all faltered.

The New England Patriots and Chicago Bears went from bottom of their division to Super Bowl contenders, with the Patriots going all the way to the big game.

There, they were dominated by Seattle, whose quarterback Sam Darnold completed his own redemption story by leading the Seahawks to their first NFL championship in 12 years.

So what lies in store this year in the NFL? Here are five things to look out for during a 2026 season that begins this week.

The Los Angeles Rams had three gripping games with divisional rivals Seattle last season, with the Seahawks winning the latter to clinch the NFC Conference before winning Super Bowl 60.

This season's big game will be played at LA's SoFi Stadium. The last time it was held there in 2022, the Rams went all-in to build a star-studded roster capable of becoming NFL champions in their own stadium.

The gamble paid off as they won Super Bowl 56. Now the Rams have tried to replicate that formula by pulling off what has been described as the greatest off-season in NFL history., external

They had last season's best offence, with quarterback Matt Stafford named the season MVP, and have practically played fantasy football in a bid to rebuild their defence and this time get the better of Seattle.

They made trades for cornerback Trent McDuffie and Myles Garrett, who claimed a record 23 sacks last season, moves which cemented the Rams as Super Bowl favourites.

Aside from the two times when the NFL MVP was a defensive player, this is the first time that a team will have both the reigning MVP (Stafford) and defensive player of the year (Garrett).

After training with the Rams over the summer, three-time defensive player of the year Aaron Donald, 35, then confirmed he would be coming out of retirement, meaning the Rams' defence will feature two of the best pass rushers of the modern era.

Before last season, Kansas City reached five Super Bowls in six years, winning three of them.

But for the first time in 11 years, coach Andy Reid failed to lead them into the play-offs, and in the game that sealed their fate, quarterback Patrick Mahomes suffered his first major injury.

There was speculation veteran tight end Travis Kelce would retire so some feared it was the end of an era for the Chiefs.

But Kelce committed to at least one more year and the Chiefs signed Kenneth Walker, who had just become the first running back to be the Super Bowl's Most Valuable Player since 1998.

For the first time in his NFL career Mahomes, 30, has an elite running back at his disposal and Walker will ease the load on the two-time season MVP as he returns from torn knee ligaments.

Mahomes also still has his go-to guy Kelce available and, after marrying Taylor Swift in the off-season, the 36-year-old can focus on helping the Chiefs bounce back in what could be his final season.

Only five active players have been named the NFL's MVP and only two are yet to win a Super Bowl - Buffalo's Josh Allen and Baltimore's Lamar Jackson.

The star quarterbacks, who were both drafted in 2018, are yet to even reach the big game, but for the first time in their NFL careers, their teams have changed their head coach.

This season marks a fresh start for the Buffalo Bills as they have promoted Joe Brady from offensive coordinator after firing Sean McDermott, as well as moving into a new 60,000-seater stadium.

Meanwhile, the Baltimore Ravens have appointed ex-Los Angeles Chargers defensive coordinator Jesse Minter to succeed John Harbaugh, who is now in charge of the New York Giants.

If Kansas City cannot get back on track, could this finally be the season that Allen or Jackson wins the AFC Conference and gets to play on the NFL's biggest stage?

The Cleveland Browns have had 13 starting quarterbacks over the past five years and the fit-again Deshaun Watson will begin the season as first choice.

The Browns signed Watson in 2022 on a five-year contract worth a guaranteed $230m (£169m) but he has played just 19 games because of injuries and a suspension over multiple sexual assault allegations.

A ruptured Achilles meant the 30-year-old missed the whole of last season, which rookie Shedeur Sanders ended as starting quarterback.

Watson was booed by Cleveland fans during a pre-season game two weeks ago, which he called "personal" and "disrespectful" before explaining that his "emotions got the best of me".

Despite that, Watson has been given one last chance to avoid going down as the worst trade in NFL history, but some believe Sanders will soon return - perhaps as early as the Browns' home opener in week three.

Sports.title: US Open 2026: Why several leading men's contenders have tumbled in New York - and why the women's draw is more stable
Sports.text:
Talent, athleticism and commitment are not nearly enough to become a Grand Slam singles champion.

Possessing the confidence that you can beat anyone on the biggest stage - where the eyes of the world are fixed on you and there is no place to hide - is arguably the most important characteristic a player can have.

Unwavering belief. Or, as former US Open runner-up Taylor Fritz describes it, delusion.

Fritz is one of the current crop of leading men yet to get his hands on one of the sport's major prizes. The world number 10 is also one of the guys who has blown what looked like a golden opportunity to win this year's US Open.

With Jannik Sinner missing through injury, and Carlos Alcaraz making his comeback from his long lay-off, it felt like a tournament where the leading seeds could capitalise.

Instead, six of the top 10 perished by the fourth round at Flushing Meadows - including Fritz, who squandered a two-set lead against Argentina's Francisco Cerundolo in round three.

Former champion Daniil Medvedev's fourth-round exit on Sunday means the only top-10 players remaining are top seed Alexander Zverev, defending champion Alcaraz and eighth seed Ben Shelton.

"It shows you how even the circuit is, how tight every match is, how difficult it is to win matches," said 24th seed Cerundolo.

"Anything can happen right now."

The dominance of Sinner and Alcaraz - who have won 10 of the past 11 Grand Slam men's singles titles between them - adds to the pressure.

Speaking to the Guardian, external earlier this year, 28-year-old Fritz said he believes he will feel an "emptiness" at the end of his career if he does not win a Grand Slam title.

World number two Zverev finally landed his first major at this year's French Open, but revealed afterwards he "could not sleep" and was "not eating" during previous Slam fortnights because of nerves.

Once he released the pressure valve, the 29-year-old German went on to reach the Wimbledon final - where he played freer but still lost to Sinner - and remains in the hunt at the US Open.

Zverev is scrambling through his half of the draw despite being far from his best, but the spectre of Alcaraz - who is getting better with every win - looms large.

"The two-horse race between Sinner and Alcaraz is not healthy for the tour," former Wimbledon champion Pat Cash told BBC Radio 5 Live.

"With every win, Alcaraz is becoming more of a favourite. Four months off, no matches and he could win the US Open."

Pressure is not the sole reason for the leading seeds tumbling in New York.

One argument is that the current top 10 - Sinner and Alcaraz aside - is weaker than it has been for a while.

Illness, injuries and fatigue also contributed at the final major of a demanding season.

Fourth seed Novak Djokovic's ageing body let him down in his shock first-round exit, while third seed Felix Auger-Aliassime put his second-round loss down to suffering dizziness.

Fifth seed Flavio Cobolli said he lacked energy in a third-round defeat, which he attributed to his volume of matches and New York's sapping heat.

Cincinnati champion Arthur Fils lost a tough opener against former world number three Stefanos Tsitsipas, while teenager Rafael Jodar - who has played more than 50 matches in his first full season on tour - looked drained during his first-round exit.

"The season is long. I think all the guys who performed well in the preparation tournaments have it more difficult here," said Belgium’s Alexander Blockx, who knocked out French Open finalist Cobolli.

"We're all human. We're not robots. Every week is difficult. Especially at a Grand Slam where it gets even more physical.

"Mentally you have to really stay in it."

The four leading players locked in a battle at Flushing Meadows for the top ranking adds another element to the dynamic.

Sabalenka has been the world number one for the past two years, but has recently suffered a dip of form which leaves her position under severe threat.

Rybakina is guaranteed to overtake Sabalenka if she reaches the semi-finals, while Pegula and Gauff could pounce if they win the title.

"Looking at the difference between the points in the top 10 compared to the men, you can see how the depth is pretty crazy," said Pegula.

"Everyone has been very consistent and makes it hard to a certain extent [to win a Slam].

"But then you know there's not one or two super dominant players where you feel like they have to lose in order for you to have a chance."

Sports.title: Manchester United v Sabah: Meet Azerbaijani club's coach Valdas Dambrauskas
Sports.text:
On Thursday, Valdas Dambrauskas will walk out at Old Trafford as manager of Sabah in the Champions League.

The Lithuanian's career will come full circle, some 20 years since he made his first steps into coaching with Manchester United Soccer Schools.

"This is beyond my imagination," Dambrauskas told BBC Sport. "To go through that tunnel on to that pitch.

"I've been many times to Old Trafford with the kids, and now I'm going to come as a coach."

This only scratches the surface of Dambrauskas' remarkable story.

It begins with an appearance on the Lithuanian version of Who Wants to Be a Millionaire?, Dambrauskas using his modest winnings to move to London and forge a career in football.

It is a tale of casual jobs, a determination to succeed and a nomadic coaching career across Europe - which now brings the 49-year-old back to England in the Champions League with the Azerbaijani club.

As Sabah's players and staff celebrated reaching the Champions League two weeks ago, unbeknownst to Dambrauskas he was becoming a social media star.

It all related to that appearance on Who Wants to Be a Millionaire? in 2002.

Not because he was on the show, but how he spent the money he won.

"This is so long ago," said Dambrauskas with a wry smile. "A back-in-the-year story that really was forgotten.

"And now suddenly everybody is speaking about this."

Dambrauskas walked away with 4,000 litas (about £725). That might not sound like much, but it was six months' wages to the average Lithuanian.

For Dambrauskas, the real story should be his career and not a game show.

"Everybody now takes only this part, you know, about the money," Dambrauskas said. "But yes, it is a true story.

"My idea was somehow I will try to go on these [coaching] courses to gain the coaching badge, maybe go back one day to Lithuania and start to work as a football coach."

What began with Who Wants to Be a Millionaire? would map out his whole career.

Dambrauskas says he had known since the age of 12 he would not make it as a player, but coaching would keep him close to football.

He arrived in London in August 2002 aged 25 on a student visa with limited English.

What followed would be eight years of hard work where he would coach for community projects, at a semi-professional club, within professional youth programmes - and hold down multiple jobs while raising two children.

In 2004 he enrolled on a course in sports science and coaching at London Metropolitan University, the first real step in his career.

Then he started out coaching by volunteering with the Access to Sports Project for deprived children in Finsbury Park.

He went on to work with London Tigers, a charitable community organisation which runs teams from junior level right through to semi-professional.

Starting out as a volunteer, across five years he progressed to manage the first team in non-league football in the Spartan South Midlands League, FA Cup and FA Vase.

Dambrauskas became the first Lithuanian to achieve a Uefa coaching licence through the London Football Association.

"I went on every possible course, every possible conference, London Football Coaches Association meetings," Dambrauskas said.

"Everywhere I could go just to gain some information, some knowledge, some extra diploma, extra course.

"That was very important for me and I took my chances."

He got his first break at a professional club when Manchester United Soccer Schools took a chance on him in 2004.

Dambrauskas spent five years coaching on residential courses in the UK and in Europe.

"That was the best thing that could happen in my life," Dambrauskas said.

"I went through three or four interviews. I will be forever grateful to [Foundation chief executive] John Shiels, the way he gave me this chance, because I didn't have experience.

"I'd never been in a place with so many great personalities as I got in the Manchester United Soccer Schools."

After a short spell with Fulham, Dambrauskas moved to Brentford. He credits academy director Ose Aibangee as one of the biggest influences on his career, pushing his limits.

All the while he was juggling home life and working multiple jobs to make ends meet.

"I was a gardener, a handyman, doing newspaper rounds at the beginning, also polishing floors in a pub," Dambrauskas said.

"So many jobs. Working in retail, and then as a sports development officer, then a sports development manager, and the central YMCA.

"I was doing two, three, sometimes four jobs."

As well as the trip to Manchester United this week, Sabah will complete their Champions League group games at Arsenal in January.

This also feels like fate for Dambrauskas - one of the buildings at London Metropolitan University on Holloway Road overlooked Emirates Stadium.

When asked about his time in England, Dambrauskas' face lights up.

"When I hear this word 'England', it for me sounds like opportunities," Dambrauskas said.

"It was really amazing. England gave me all this and I'll forever be grateful."

Dambrauskas was working three jobs - at Brentford, London Tigers and as a sports development manager - when the opportunity arose to coach full-time.

It meant leaving England to return to Lithuania, champions Ekranas appointing him assistant first-team and reserve-team coach at the end of 2010.

After four years at Ekranas he was named manager of Zalgiris Vilnius, Lithuania's biggest club, where his career really took off.

Dambrauskas won two league titles, three Lithuanian Cups and two Lithuanian Super Cups across three seasons - including a treble in 2016.

Then came a series of moves in which Dambrauskas took charge of eight teams over nine years in seven countries.

First RFS, with whom he won the Latvian Cup, and then Gorica in Croatia.

A third league title came with Bulgarian side Ludogorets Razgrad, along with another Super Cup and Europa League qualification.

Dambrauskas then returned to Croatia with Hajduk Split, a time which he described as "absolutely amazing" as the club won the Croatian Cup - their first trophy for 10 years.

Next up was a spell in Greece with OFI Crete, then Omonia in Cyprus - who qualified for the Conference League - and Diosgyori in Hungary.

Finally, in the summer of 2025, he arrived at Sabah, the 10th club of his career.

Dambrauskas completed the league and cup double in his first season, as the club won the title for the first time.

It took his trophy tally to 13 across five countries.

Next stop, the Champions League.

Dambrauskas had to navigate four knockout ties to get Sabah to the Champions League, and they are the only club to make it all the way through from the first qualifying round.

Welsh club TNS, Finland's KuPS, Danish side Aarhus and Israel's Hapoel Beer-Sheva were all knocked out.

The final qualifying game was as dramatic as Dambrauskas' own story.

Sabah were going out, then a goal by Tellur Mutallimov in the fourth minute of stoppage time sent the tie into extra time. They went on to win 5-2 on the night and 6-4 on aggregate.

"To go to the Champions League is something beyond imagination," Dambrauskas said.

"We have never qualified for the Conference League, we have never qualified for the Europa League. We have never passed more than two rounds in a row in one competition, and now suddenly we are here."

Sabah are based in the town of Masazir - 30 miles north of the Azerbaijan capital Baku - with a population of just 19,000.

Known as the Owls, Sabah were only formed in 2017 and on Tuesday will celebrate their ninth birthday.

Like many small clubs, their Bank Respublika Arena home, with a capacity of less than 9,000, does not meet Uefa regulations. Instead, the club are expected to play their matches at the Olympic Stadium in Baku.

Sabah will host Borussia Dortmund, Barcelona and Napoli, and face a trip to Villarreal - as well as the visits to England.

"It can be a very hard draw, and it can be a Sabah draw," said Dambrauskas, clearly excited by the prospect.

"You dream for this, to play in this competition, to play against those teams.

"So now is the time to show that you can handle it, to find a way to compete and we will try to do this.

"We have a good team, we have an ambitious team, we have hungry players who are really keen to show themselves."

Sabah president Magsud Adigozalov last week was full of praise for Dambrauskas' impact.

"His influence goes beyond tactics," Adigozalov told Report. "He has instilled a mindset and winning mentality in the team.

"Even in the most difficult moments, the team never abandons its game or fighting spirit, which is the result of the coach's work."

Twenty years ago, Dambrauskas looked out over the pitch at Old Trafford during one of his job interviews, dreaming that one day he would stand in one of the dugouts.

Now his coaching career will return to where it started.

"I lived in England when the battle between Manchester United and Arsenal was the biggest rivalry. Alex Ferguson and Arsene Wenger," Dambrauskas said.

"Now I'm going to come back as a coach in the Champions League and hear that anthem. It's really amazing."
